READING THE FORECAST

Conviction.
With perspective.

01 /

Shared errors matter.

A strong House lean does not guarantee a Senate sweep. My Senate winner map is 53 Democratic-aligned seats; the plausible average is closer to 51–52. Close races can break together.

02 /

People split their tickets.

Kansas, Iowa and Texas have different governor and Senate outlooks. Candidate strength and local conditions matter alongside the national environment.

03 /

Receipts over reach.

Fabricated firms are excluded from original-poll review. Source transparency matters. Social engagement and early-vote registration are never treated as candidate votes.

OPEN THE NOTEBOOK

How this forecast was made.

This is an editorial forecast, not an election-results service or a professionally backtested statistical model. The cutoff is November 3 at 3:22 p.m. CST. No early partial returns were used.

Election Day review · 3:22 p.m. CST

All race favorites and national totals are unchanged. The new Iowa PAC poll has incomplete regional weighting; daytime turnout reports do not reveal candidate votes. Georgia’s official turnout hub does not update during Election Day. The earlier 5:55 review was in the morning; its previous p.m. label was incorrect.

Weight evidence, not volume

Original Siena, Emerson, Marquette, UNH and GMU releases receive priority. Field dates, sample, sponsor, ballot wording and transparent methods matter. Multiple models using the same poll are not independent confirmation.

What was excluded

Wedgewood and Median Strategies receive zero weight in original-poll review. Unverified late releases, partisan informed-ballot experiments, social likes and anecdotes do not determine the forecast. The third-party House baseline cannot be independently certified free of every contaminated input without its raw archives; this is not a clean-room re-aggregation of every poll.

How the numbers work

House: Call the Map’s November 2 district baseline, with explicit narrow winner changes in MI-10, PA-01, IA-03 and FL-22 and confidence revisions in other competitive seats. Senate and governors: independent candidate-level judgments, checked against original polling and state fundamentals. Probabilities describe my uncertainty and are not claims of fitted calibration. No number under 60% is a comfortable lead.

My broad control assessments: House Democrats about 90%; Democratic-aligned Senate about 65%. Judgmental plausible ranges: House 220–252 D, Senate 47–55 Democratic-aligned, governors 25–31 D. These are not calibrated confidence intervals. The favorite map can differ from a simulated or probability-weighted average. Statewide slider margins are illustrative equivalents derived from my confidence ratings; they are not predicted vote shares.

Geography & election mechanics

435 voting House districts use Census 120th Congress geometry, except Missouri, which uses the 119th map following the court-ordered reversion. Alaska and Hawaii are inset at lower left. State borders are simplified Census cartography. In Alaska and Maine, ranked-choice rules can affect the final winner. Vermont requires a majority or legislative selection. Louisiana’s crowded House primaries can advance to a December 12 runoff; LA-05 and LA-06 are party forecasts with the eventual individual winner unresolved.

Social media and early voting

Public indexed posts and local reporting were checked. Coverage of X and Reddit was incomplete, not exhaustive; private communities and unindexed material were not accessed. Ralston’s Nevada work is a useful weak cross-check. Party registration does not reveal how a ballot was cast. No numerical social-engagement adjustment was used.

Photo coverage

Real candidate portraits are used when sourced. A labeled initials fallback appears where no verified photo is available. Photos are never generated, substituted from another person or portrayed as endorsements.
